turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good morning, Ms. Alvarez. Today we will go over the treatment plan for the next few weeks.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Thank you. I am so scared. I do not really understand what happened to her blood.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Mia’s bone marrow was making too many unhealthy white blood cells. This is called acute lymphoblastic leukemia. It is the most common childhood leukemia, and there is a well-tested treatment plan.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: How long does it last? Will she be able to go back to school?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Treatment has several phases over about two years. The first phase is called induction. It uses chemo through her port, and pills at home, with clinic visits every week.

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Is the needle going to hurt?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: The nurses are very good at it. Ms. Alvarez, Mia will take mercaptopurine pills every night at bedtime.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: Okay. She isn’t on any other medicines, just those pills.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good. Her blood counts can drop with chemo, so she may catch infections more easily. Keep her away from sick kids.

turns.speaker: caregiver
turns.text: I’m sorry, what does that mean, her counts?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: We will check her labs every week. Any other questions?

turns.speaker: child
turns.text: Did I get sick because I was bad?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That is a good question, sweetheart. Okay, the nurse will bring the paperwork.
